head:
Seniors · Ageing

How the body ages

Everyone knows the body ages. Few people know what declines, at what age, how fast, and above all what depends on you. This article starts from a simple question, states it clearly, then answers it in six steps, from the general picture to particular cases, with the objections and what remains uncertain.

The question

You probably know two people of the same age, one who climbs the stairs without thinking and one who holds on to the handrail. The usual answer is: “it's age.” That answer hides two different ideas. The first: the body would decline along a single, steady slope that nobody can bend. The second: it would decline piece by piece, each at its own pace, some very early, others late and abruptly, and some of these slopes would change depending on what you do.

This is not a quarrel over words. If the first idea is right, there is nothing to measure before it happens and little to do. If the second is right, movements that can be measured from 40 or 50 years old foreshadow what follows, and actions change the trajectory. Studies allow us to settle this in part. At each step, I say what is established and what is not.

The question

Is the ageing of the body a single slope that you simply endure, or a sum of slopes, a large part of which can be measured early and worked on? And if it is the second, which ones should you watch, at what age, and what should you do?

What is at stake

The first stake is independence. According to the World Health Organization, 28 to 35% of people aged 65 and over fall each year, and 32 to 42% of those over 70.15 A fall is not a simple misstep: it is the event that turns a decline in balance or strength, invisible until then, into an injury.

The typical injury is the hip fracture. According to the International Osteoporosis Foundation (IOF), up to 20 to 24% of patients die within the year, 40% can no longer walk alone a year later and 33% are totally dependent or in an institution. The same page notes that 80% are limited in activities such as driving or doing their shopping, and that fractures can lead to depression and isolation.11 This is an organisation page with no original study: an order of magnitude of severity, not a forecast for you.

This goes beyond health in the medical sense. Getting up on your own, carrying your shopping, climbing the stairs at home, playing with your grandchildren or continuing a recreational sport: all of this relies on strength, speed and balance, and is lost in steps. The earlier you see the step, the more room there is to act.

The second stake is lifespan: walking speed, getting up from the floor and grip strength are associated with survival in large cohorts (step 5). The third is performance: what you will do at 70 is built partly at 40 or 50. This is a deduction from the steps that follow, not a study result.

Finally, the problem is silent. Weight can stay stable while muscle melts away and fat replaces it.24 The first sign is often the fall itself, that is, the moment when it is too late to measure. This is why the question cannot be left unanswered.

The demonstration

The reasoning goes from the most general to the most precise: the shape of the curves across the whole population, then muscle, endurance, bone and hormones (with the differences between sexes), then what these declines foreshadow, then the objections, and finally what randomised trials allow us to state.

Step 1Ageing is not a single slope

Claim: each capacity has its own trajectory, and it even changes depending on how it is measured.

First clue, grip strength, measured by squeezing a dynamometer. Dodds and colleagues pooled 12 British general-population studies, a total of 49,964 people. Strength rises to a peak (51 kg median in men between 29 and 39 years, 31 kg in women between 26 and 42 years), holds, then declines from midlife. At 80, 23% of men and 27% of women have “weak” strength, that is, at least 2.5 standard deviations below the average peak for their sex.1 This threshold is severe: these people have lost far more than the average. The peak is reached before the forties and the decline starts in midlife, not at retirement.

Second clue, balance. Springer and colleagues measured how long 549 healthy adults, aged 18 to 99, can stand on one leg, taking the best of three trials. Once looking ahead, once with eyes closed, which removes vision and forces the body to rely on the inner ear and the sense of position.2

With eyes closed, balance declines decades earlier than with eyes open

Derived figures: each mean time is divided by that of the 18-39 year olds in the same condition (44.7 s eyes open, 15.2 s eyes closed) then multiplied by 100, to compare two curve shapes. The raw times are in the source. 98 to 101 people per age group (59 for the 80-99 year olds), men and women combined. Source: Springer et al., Journal of Geriatric Physical Therapy.2

What this means

With eyes open, the mean holds at around 41 to 45 seconds up to 59 years, then falls to 32.1, 21.5 and 9.4 seconds. With eyes closed, it has already lost nearly half at 50-59 years (8.3 seconds versus 15.2). The authors note this too.2 A test taken at 45 with eyes open can therefore reassure you even though the capacity that compensates when vision is missing (in the dark, on uneven ground) has already declined. There is not one ageing curve, but one per capacity and per condition.

A review by Macaluso and De Vito places peak strength between the second and third decades, followed by a decline of about 12 to 15% per decade, faster after 65.3 This comes mostly from studies that compare different ages: step 6 explains why that matters.

Where this leads. If the slopes differ, we need to see what produces them. We start with muscle, which gets you up, lets you climb a step and catches you when you trip.

Step 2Muscle: strength goes faster than mass, power faster than strength

Claim: what is lost first is not the volume of the muscle but its ability to produce force, especially quickly.

The medical definition reflects this. The EWGSOP2 European consensus describes sarcopenia as a muscle disease rooted in unfavourable changes that accumulate over a lifetime. Low strength is its central criterion; low muscle quantity or quality confirms the diagnosis; poor physical performance signals a severe form.6 In other words, what the muscle does matters more than what it weighs.

Goodpaster and colleagues followed 1,880 older adults for three years. Leg lean mass declines by about 1% a year; leg strength by 2.6 to 4.1% a year depending on the group, about three times faster. Gaining lean mass did not prevent strength from declining, which the authors attribute to a decline in muscle quality.4

Leg strength declines about three times faster than leg lean mass

Mean decline per year over three years in 1,880 older adults, by the groups defined by the study (sex and ethnic origin). Lean mass (about 1% a year) is given as a single figure in the source. Source: Goodpaster et al., Journals of Gerontology A, 2006 (abstract).4

What this means

Your muscle mass does not tell your strength: you can keep the volume and lose the capacity. The mirror and the scales are therefore not enough; only a measured movement (squeezing, getting up, pushing) tells you where the muscle stands.

Strength is only half of it. Power is strength multiplied by speed: it gets you up quickly from a chair and catches you when you trip. Skelton and colleagues compared 50 healthy men and 50 healthy women aged 65 to 89: isometric strength declines by about 1 to 2% a year, leg power by about 3.5%. The difference is significant in men (p = 0.0001), not in the women of the sample (p = 0.08). Power relative to body weight is linked to the time taken to get up from a low chair.5 Macaluso and De Vito agree: power is more vulnerable than strength, with selective atrophy of the fast fibres.3 These cohorts differ and the rates cannot be compared one to one; the direction is the same.

How many people are affected depends on the definition. A meta-analysis of 151 studies (692,056 participants, mean age 68.5 years) finds 10 to 27% sarcopenia depending on the classification, and the direction of the difference between sexes reverses: 11% of men versus 2% of women with EWGSOP2, 17% of women versus 12% of men with the criteria of the International Working Group on Sarcopenia.7 A “percentage of sarcopenic seniors” means nothing without its definition.

Where this leads. Muscle is half the engine. The other half supplies it with oxygen. Here, studies have followed the same people for years, and the results are less comfortable.

Step 3Endurance: a slope that accelerates, and a huge gap between profiles

Claim: VO2max declines at every age, faster and faster, and the speed of this decline varies greatly depending on the profile.

VO2max is the maximum rate of oxygen your body can use, the reference measure of endurance. Fleg and colleagues followed 810 adults aged 21 to 87 (375 women, 435 men), without heart disease, with repeated treadmill measurements, over a median of 7 to 9 years. VO2max declines in every decade, from about 3 to 6% per decade in the twenties and thirties to more than 20% per decade from 70 years. Men decline faster from the forties.8

A point that is uncomfortable: the acceleration is similar across all quarters of self-reported physical activity, “regardless of physical activity” according to the authors. To be read with care: the activity was self-reported, so coarse, and the sample is not made up of athletes.8

To know what training changes, you need people who train: Burtscher and colleagues reviewed follow-ups of veteran athletes (“masters”). In healthy sedentary adults, VO2max declines by about 10% per decade after 25 to 30 years. In masters men who maintain their training volume, the decline is 5 to 6.5% per decade. When volume falls by 11 to 20%, the range is 8 to 26%. When it falls by more than 20% or they become almost sedentary, it ranges from 15 to 46%. The change in training volume explains 54% of the variance in the decline in men and 39% in women.9

The decline in endurance per decade ranges from a few points to more than 40% depending on the profile

Solid bar: bottom of the range. Light bar: up to the top of the range. The ranges for masters come from small groups of men with different methods: orders of magnitude. Sources: Fleg et al., Circulation, 2005 (report); Burtscher et al., Int J Environ Res Public Health, 2022.8,9

What this means

Two readings hold together. The slope accelerates with age in both sources, and even athletes who train relentlessly lose something: 5 to 6.5% per decade, and 4.1% in cross-country skiers aged 58.7 who kept competing (a figure from another study cited by the review).9 But the gap between profiles is far larger than this incompressible part. What you keep doing between 40 and 60 weighs on what you will be able to do at 70.

According to the review, these changes follow those of maximal cardiac output. Stopping training lowers VO2max by about 20% in 12 weeks; resuming raises it quickly (about 29% in 84 days in men of about 68 years, in one study). Part of the “age-related decline” of those who slow down is therefore due to stopping.9

The review acknowledges its limits: a few groups of men, little data on women, incomplete mechanisms.9 I therefore cannot put a figure on the avoidable part of Fleg's acceleration. It is partly avoidable, otherwise the gaps between masters would not exist.

Where this leads. Muscle and endurance are tested with a stopwatch or on a treadmill. The skeleton and hormones call for another scale, and this is where the trajectories of men and women diverge the most.

Step 4Bone and hormones: trajectories that differ by sex

Claim: bone peaks very early and its loss accelerates at the age of menopause, whereas men have a slow hormonal decline. Neither can be seen.

According to the Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation, peak bone mass is reached between 18 and 25 years. In the five to seven years after menopause, women can lose up to 20% or more of their bone density, because oestrogen falls. Loss also accelerates in midlife in men. The page does not cite the original study: 20% is a plausible maximum, not an average.10 The median age of natural menopause is 50 years (range of 48 to 53 for the middle half of women).13

This loss is silent, then it becomes a disease. Approximate share of women affected by osteoporosis worldwide, according to the IOF: about one in ten at 60, one in five at 70, two in five at 80, two in three at 90.12

Osteoporosis affects few women at 60, then the share climbs faster and faster

Approximate proportions given by the IOF (worldwide) without specified criteria or studies; the heights are derived from these fractions (10, 20, 40 and about 67%). Source: International Osteoporosis Foundation, epidemiology page.12

What this means

Between 60 and 80 the share is multiplied by four, then it goes from 2 in 5 to 2 in 3 between 80 and 90. Low density cannot be felt: only a medical examination (bone densitometry) measures it, and no fitness test replaces it. The IOF also estimates that one woman in three and one man in five over 50 will have a fracture due to osteoporosis.11

In men, the decline is gentler. Harman and colleagues followed 890 healthy men: total testosterone falls by about 0.124 nmol/L a year, and about 20% of those over 60, 30% of those over 70 and 50% of those over 80 would be hypogonadal. It also falls with body mass index, and the abstract leaves open the share due to diseases and medication.14

The American Heart Association statement on menopause adds nuance: lipids change rather with menopause; blood pressure, insulin and blood glucose rather with age. After menopause, there is more visceral fat and less lean mass.13 Between the sexes, there is no simple winner: “weak” grip strength at 80 is close (23 versus 27%),1 sarcopenia changes direction depending on the definition,7 VO2max declines faster in men from 40 years.8 Only bone shows a clear gap, on the women's side.

Where this leads. We know what declines and at what pace. It remains to see whether these declines translate into concrete events, and whether simple movements foreshadow them.

Step 5From the number to the movement: what simple measures foreshadow

Claim: movements that can be measured in one minute are associated with serious events, from falls to survival.

Balance: Springer reports, from another study (Vellas) that I have not read, that those who cannot hold 5 seconds on one leg have 2.1 times the risk of a fall with injury.2 This is a second-hand figure.

Walking speed: Studenski and colleagues pooled 9 studies (34,485 adults aged 65 and over, mean age 73.5 years, 6 to 21 years of follow-up, 17,528 deaths). Speeds of 1.0 m/s or more are associated with longer survival than expected for age and sex, speeds below 0.6 m/s with an increased risk of early death.16

Getting up from the floor: Araujo and colleagues scored 2,002 adults aged 51 to 80 out of 10 points (5 for sitting down, 5 for getting up, one point fewer for each support of a hand or knee). Over a median of 6.3 years, 159 died, of whom only two among those who scored 10. A score below 8 is associated with 2 to 5 times more deaths, and each additional point with 21% lower mortality.17

Grip strength: the PURE study (139,691 adults aged 35 to 70, 17 countries, median 4 years) associates each 5 kg decline with a risk of death multiplied by 1.16 (1.13 to 1.20), and strength predicts mortality better than systolic pressure in a post hoc analysis.18

What this means

These are indicators, not causes. Getting up without your hands does not protect you: it reflects a body that keeps strength, power, balance and mobility, and a person who is ill, sometimes without knowing it, does it less well. Their value is practical: one minute of measurement, comparable with yourself from one year to the next.

Where this leads. An indicator is not a lever. Before concluding that we can act, we need to go through the objections, then see whether, when people are drawn at random to train, their fate changes.

Step 6The objections, and what training really changes

Claim: part of the decline is incompressible, but randomised trials show a real effect of exercise on the risk of falls and on muscle. Some effects are more modest than is said, and others remain unproven.

Objection 1: the curves compare people of different ages

This is the case for many figures, including those of Springer and Macaluso. A cross-sectional study mixes age with generation, lifestyle and survival. According to Macaluso, follow-ups of the same people find a faster decline than comparisons between ages;3 Fleg's commentators note that cross-sectional studies can overestimate the maintenance of fitness.8 If there is a bias, it therefore makes the picture too optimistic: that is my reading, not the authors'. Averages predict nothing for a given person.

Objection 2: it's age, not activity

Three results point in this direction: the acceleration of VO2max in Fleg regardless of self-reported activity,8 the strength that declines despite a gain in mass in Goodpaster,4 and the 4.1% per decade of skiers who kept competing.9 A part therefore escapes control. Counter-example: the University of Birmingham press release on the study by Pollock and Duggal (2018) describes 125 amateur cyclists aged 55 to 79, compared with 75 inactive adults aged 57 to 80 and 55 young people aged 20 to 36. No age-related loss of muscle or strength in the cyclists, testosterone remaining high in the men.23 But they are highly selected (smokers, heavy drinkers and people with illnesses excluded), the comparison is cross-sectional and the press release gives no figures: this shows what is possible, not what is typical.

Objection 3: improving an indicator does not necessarily change the event

Correct: no source read here shows that improving your walking speed, grip strength or getting up from the floor lengthens life. Randomised trials (participants drawn at random between exercise and comparison) look at closer events: falls, muscle, bone.

What the trials say

Falls first. The review by Sherrington and colleagues pools 108 randomised trials, 23,407 adults aged 60 and over living at home (mean age 76 years, 77% women). With all exercise types combined, the rate of falls is multiplied by 0.77, that is 23% lower (59 trials, interval 0.71 to 0.83, high certainty). Balance and functional training alone: 0.76 (39 trials, high certainty); with strength training: 0.66 (11 trials, moderate certainty). In those over 75: 0.83. For 850 falls over a year without exercise, the authors estimate 195 fewer falls (144 to 246).19

For 1,000 people, exercise avoids about 195 falls a year

Derived figure: 655 = 850 minus 195, as calculated by the authors (interval of 144 to 246 falls avoided). The 850 is the reference rate used in the record, not a rate observed for you. Source: Sherrington et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2020 (PEDro record).19

What this means

This is the strongest result in the whole article: randomised trials, high certainty, and an effect that also exists after 75. It is an average: it guarantees nothing for you. Adding strength training gives a lower rate (0.66 versus 0.76), but the confidence intervals overlap and the authors do not set them directly against each other in this summary.

Muscle next. Peterson and colleagues (49 studies, 1,328 participants aged 50 and over) estimate that resistance training adds on average 1.1 kg of lean mass (0.9 to 1.2). Higher-volume programmes produce larger gains, the oldest gain less, and the studies differ a great deal (I² = 84%).20 Set this beside Goodpaster: gaining mass does not protect strength for certain, so function is what to aim for.

Bone, finally, with the most modest effect. Kelley and colleagues pool 25 studies in 1,775 inactive postmenopausal women (mean age 62-63 years): a small but clear effect on the femoral neck (effect size 0.288, interval 0.102 to 0.474), and on the lumbar spine an effect of 0.179 whose interval touches zero (−0.003 to 0.361). The authors deduce by calculation about 10 to 11% lower fracture risk at 20 years, without observed fracture data.21 A network meta-analysis of 19 trials (919 women over 50) gives the best results for moderate strength training three days a week, with trials of moderate quality and an advantage that is no longer significant beyond 48 weeks.22

What remains unproven: that improving an indicator reduces mortality; jump or sprint power at 40-50, for which I have no reliable figure; the effect of hormone treatments, which this article does not assess; individual thresholds of normality at each age.

The answer to the question

Ageing is not a single slope. Balance with eyes open holds until about 59 then falls, with eyes closed it declines from the forties; grip strength and bone peak before 40 and 25 years; strength goes about three times faster than mass, power faster than strength; VO2max declines faster and faster, from 3 to 6% per decade in the twenties to more than 20% after 70.

A part is endured, and I cannot put a figure on it: the best veterans still lose 4 to 6.5% of VO2max per decade. But the gap between profiles (5 to 46% per decade) far exceeds this part, and exercise reduces falls by about a quarter, including after 75. Level of certainty:

  • Solid (randomised trials, high certainty): exercise reduces falls by about a quarter.
  • Probable (trials or follow-ups, with limits): strength training adds lean mass (+1.1 kg on average); the decline in endurance depends a great deal on the volume kept; strength and power decline faster than mass.
  • Modest: the effect of exercise on bone density, small at the femoral neck and uncertain at the spine.
  • Not established: that improving walking speed, grip strength or getting up from the floor lengthens life; the exact share of the decline due to age alone.

The answer fits in one sentence: several slopes, some of which can be measured early and worked on with a demonstrated effect on falls and muscle, others only attenuated, and a part remains unquantified.

What to put in place

  1. Take a first measurement at 40 or 50, not at 70.A single number gives a level; two numbers spaced apart show a trajectory. The movements of step 5 (balance with eyes open and closed, getting up from a chair or the floor, grip strength, walking speed, endurance test) can be measured without heavy equipment. Bone density and muscle mass require a medical examination.
  2. Repeat the same measurement every one to two years, under the same conditions.Same shoes, same floor, same time of day. This frequency is an editorial recommendation: no source read sets it.
  3. Work on balance and legs first.Balance and functional training reduces falls (0.76), with strength training 0.66.19
  4. Do strength training, with volume and speed.Higher-volume programmes add more lean mass.20 For bone, the dose studied is moderate strength training (65 to 80% of maximum load) three days a week, in women over 50.22 Since power declines first, movements performed quickly have their place.
  5. Keep your endurance volume.The decline in VO2max deepens when volume falls by more than 20% or stops, not when you slow down a little.9

The tests on this page give you the first measurement and the means to repeat it. Chest pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or a recent fall justify medical advice before any test or harder training.

What these figures do not say
  • Many curves compare different ages at the same time and mix age, generation and survival. Averages do not give an individual trajectory.
  • Several figures on bone come from organisation pages with no original study, and the links between simple movements and survival are associations.

Frequently asked questions

If part of the decline is unavoidable, what is the point of training?

Because the gap between profiles is larger than the incompressible part: 5 to 46% decline in VO2max per decade among masters,9 and about a quarter fewer falls with exercise.19

My weight hasn't moved: has my muscle not either?

Not necessarily: fat can increase while muscle decreases.24 After menopause, the AHA reports more visceral fat and less lean mass.13

Can an 80-year-old still improve?

The review on falls showed an effect in those over 75.19 It does not say by how much a specific capacity improves in an individual.
